clue.text: Futile endeavour roughing up floor with sander

indicators.note: to rough something up is to knock it about, so the letters that follow are knocked out of order

blocks.note: taken as written
joins the two words of the fodder
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone decides sanding the floor is pointless after tearing it up with the machine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Floor sander' looks like a tool in a DIY scene, but its eleven letters are the raw material.
explanation.definitionFit: A fool's errand is an idiom for a task with no hope of success, a pointless undertaking.

clue.text: See 28
Mollusc soup cooked by our chef today for starters

indicators.note: cooking transforms ingredients, so these letters are mixed into a new order
starters are the openings, so only the first letter of each word counts

blocks.note: taken as written
the initial letters of our, chef and today

explanation.surface: A seafood soup prepared by the chef as today's starter.
explanation.definitionFit: An octopus is an eight-armed cephalopod, a class of mollusc despite having no shell.

clue.text: Sounds like a hit from Bugsy Malone

definitions.text: Sounds like a hit from Bugsy Malone

blocks.clueFragment: Sounds like a hit from Bugsy Malone
blocks.note: surface: a hit song from the musical film Bugsy Malone
setter's reading: the noise of a blow, the wet impact of the custard-firing splurge guns in that film

explanation.walkthrough: Bugsy Malone is a 1976 gangster musical with child actors whose guns fire cream; 'hit' suggests a chart song but means a strike, and the answer is the noise it makes.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is an onomatopoeic name for the sound of something soft and wet striking a surface.

clue.text: Good old Bluth's highly profitable venture?

blocks.note: G is the standard abbreviation for good
taken as written
Bluth is the setter, so the setter's thing is, from the setter's mouth, 'mine'

explanation.surface: The setter boasts that this puzzle is a lucrative old money-spinner.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters often name themselves in a clue; the possessive turns into the first-person 'mine'.
explanation.definitionFit: A gold mine is used figuratively for any enterprise yielding large returns, a source of great wealth.

clue.text: Putting gift outside large door — finally giving hint

indicators.note: putting one word outside another wraps it around the other
finally picks out the very last letter

blocks.note: a gimme is something easy, a gift, as in a conceded putt in golf
L is the abbreviation for large
the final letter of door

explanation.surface: Someone wraps a present round a big door, which gives away a clue.
explanation.walkthrough: L sits inside GIMME after its first letter; R then goes on the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A glimmer of something is a faint sign or trace of it, close in sense to a hint.

clue.text: Set up arrest as practical joke

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means read from the bottom, so backwards

blocks.note: to set is to gel, as jelly does
to pull is slang for to arrest

explanation.surface: A fake arrest is staged as a prank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set up' reads as one phrase meaning to frame, but 'up' is the reversal signal for this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A leg-pull is a hoax or joke played on someone, from the idiom 'pull someone's leg'.

clue.text: Tool for moving garden waste from meadow — e.g. rose bush's first cutting

indicators.note: first picks out only the opening letter of the word before it
a piece cutting into something sits inside it, splitting the word around it

blocks.note: lea is a poetic word for a meadow
a rose is an example of a flower
the opening letter of bush

explanation.surface: A gardener needs something to clear away the clippings after pruning a rose bush in the meadow.
explanation.walkthrough: The B goes inside FLOWER just after its first letter, giving F-B-LOWER.
explanation.definitionFit: A leaf blower is a powered garden machine that pushes fallen leaves and debris into piles by air.

clue.text: Property in Spain changes when roof comes off

indicators.note: in a down clue the roof is the top, so the opening letter is lost

blocks.note: E is the international vehicle code for Spain
affects means changes or influences

explanation.surface: A Spanish house is altered when its roof is removed.
explanation.definitionFit: Effects means personal belongings, as in 'personal effects', so it is a synonym for property.

clue.text: See 30
Parodist — to some extent, aim it at original

indicators.note: to some extent means only partly, so the word lies within part of the phrase

blocks.note: runs across the four words

explanation.surface: Advice to a satirist: direct your mockery at the original work.
explanation.definitionFit: A parodist mimics another's style for comic effect, so is a kind of copier or mimic.

clue.text: Former partner ringing — praising …

blocks.note: an ex is a former partner
a bell tolling is ringing

explanation.surface: An ex phones up, full of compliments, and the sentence trails into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links this clue's surface to the next one; it plays no part in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To extol is to praise lavishly, so extolling is a synonym for praising in the same -ing form.

clue.text: … crime syndicate backing plan framing group of footballers

indicators.note: a frame goes round a picture, so one word surrounds the other
backing means moving in the opposite direction, so the result is read right to left

blocks.note: an aim is a plan or intention
the FA is the Football Association

explanation.surface: Gangsters back a scheme to frame a football team, continuing the ex-partner story.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis carries the surface on from the previous clue; 'backing' applies to the whole framed result, not just the plan.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mafia is the best-known organised crime network, the archetypal criminal syndicate.

clue.text: Finish off a bespoke costume with a hat and facial hair?

indicators.note: bespoke clothing is made to order, so these letters are tailored into a new shape

blocks.note: to zap is to kill, to finish off
taken as written
taken as written
joins the fodder pieces
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone completes a made-to-measure fancy-dress outfit by adding a hat and a false moustache.
explanation.walkthrough: A Zapata moustache is a thick drooping style named after the Mexican revolutionary Emiliano Zapata.
explanation.definitionFit: The question mark flags the definition as one example: this moustache is one kind of facial hair.

clue.text: I weep with soldiers returning to front line

indicators.note: returning means going back the way it came, so the word is read backwards

blocks.note: taken as written
to sob is to weep
simply joins the pieces
RA is the Royal Artillery

explanation.surface: A soldier's sweetheart cries as the troops go back to the front.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Front line' sounds military, but it is the weather map's front line: isobars are drawn as lines on a weather chart.
explanation.definitionFit: An isobar is a line on a weather map joining points of equal pressure, and fronts are mapped alongside them.

clue.text: Wife leaving weakling for trouble-maker

indicators.note: something leaving goes away, so that letter is taken out

blocks.note: W is the abbreviation for wife
a wimp is a feeble person

explanation.surface: A wife walks out on her feeble husband, causing trouble.
explanation.definitionFit: An imp is a mischievous little devil, hence a playfully naughty troublemaker.

clue.text: Runs Merseyside town golf shop originally

indicators.note: originally takes things at their origin, the first letter of each word

blocks.note: Bootle is a town just north of Liverpool in Merseyside
the initial letters of golf and shop

explanation.surface: A list of a Merseyside town's businesses, its golf shop first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runs' looks like a verb about managing a shop; it means smuggles.
explanation.definitionFit: To bootleg goods is to make or carry them illegally, as to run contraband.

clue.text: News from pilates teacher

indicators.note: the answer comes out of the words that follow, lifted from inside them

blocks.note: runs across the two words

explanation.surface: Gossip picked up from an exercise instructor.
explanation.definitionFit: The latest is a noun meaning the most recent news or developments, as in 'have you heard the latest?'

clue.text: Article in Times is junk

indicators.note: one piece goes in another, enclosed by it

blocks.note: T is short for time, so two times make TT
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece is dismissed as rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: Tat is British slang for cheap, tasteless goods or rubbish, matching junk.

clue.text: Beano cancelled after putting out extremely racist punchline

indicators.note: extremely points at the extremes of the word, its first and last letters
putting something out ejects it, so those letters are removed

blocks.note: a beano is British slang for a party or celebration
the first and last letters of racist
an event that is off has been cancelled

explanation.surface: A comic's party booking is scrapped once an offensive joke is cut.
explanation.walkthrough: Beano is also the name of a British children's comic, which suits the joke surface; here it means a party.
explanation.definitionFit: A pay-off is the climax of a story or joke, the line delivering the laugh.

clue.text: You're welcome in new amenity

indicators.note: something new is made afresh, so the letters are put in a fresh order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A greeting for visitors to a new facility.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying 'any time' in reply to thanks is an idiom equivalent to 'you're welcome'.

clue.text: Dropped in on independent film director

blocks.note: fell is the past of fall, dropped
taken as written
I is the abbreviation for independent

explanation.surface: Someone paid a visit to an indie film-maker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dropped in on' reads as one phrase for visiting; it splits into separate pieces. Federico Fellini was an Italian director (La Dolce Vita).
explanation.definitionFit: Fellini was a celebrated Italian director of films such as 8½, so he is an example of a film director.

clue.text: Most painful — well, put your feet up

blocks.note: 'so' and 'well' are both sentence-opening fillers
to put your feet up is to rest

explanation.surface: Advice to someone in pain: well then, sit down and relax.
explanation.definitionFit: Sore means painful, and sorest is its superlative, matching 'most painful' exactly.

clue.text: Fear and admire cycling

indicators.note: cycling means going round, so letters move from the front of the word to the back

blocks.note: to respect is to admire

explanation.surface: Someone feels both terror and awe while riding a bike.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening RE moves to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A spectre is a ghost, or figuratively a looming threat or dread, as in 'the spectre of war'.

clue.text: Perhaps King Charles's plausible story about a knight

indicators.note: about means around, so one word wraps the other

blocks.note: a spiel is a glib, persuasive patter
taken as written
N is the chess notation for knight

explanation.surface: The King's tale about a knight sounds believable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'King Charles' suggests the monarch; here it is the King Charles spaniel, a small dog breed, and 's means 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: The King Charles spaniel is a toy dog breed, so 'perhaps' marks it as one example of the dog.

clue.text: See 1
See 6
Somehow Ally Pally discovered other bar for venue

indicators.note: somehow says the letters arrive by some unstated route, rearranged
dis-covered means stripped of its cover, its outside letters taken away

blocks.note: taken as written
Pally without its first and last letters
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone discovers Alexandra Palace has another bar, as if comparing London venues.
explanation.walkthrough: Ally Pally is the nickname of Alexandra Palace, a London entertainment venue; the Royal Albert Hall is a famous London concert hall.
explanation.definitionFit: The Royal Albert Hall is a concert and events hall in Kensington, a well-known performance venue.

clue.text: Goes off short walks

blocks.note: first meaning: becomes sour, as milk does
second meaning: brief strolls, as in taking a turn round the garden

explanation.surface: Someone leaves for brief strolls.
explanation.definitionFit: Milk that turns has gone sour, and a turn is also a short stroll, so both senses share the word.

clue.text: Surviving crew no longer appearing to be getting on

indicators.note: something no longer appearing has gone missing, so it is dropped

blocks.note: managing means getting by, surviving
to man a ship is to crew it

explanation.surface: A band's remaining members have vanished from view and seem to be growing old.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting on is an idiom for growing old, so aging fits as the same present participle.

clue.text: Milan side struggle with audience?

blocks.note: Inter Milan is a famous Italian football club
to vie is to compete or struggle
W is a standard abbreviation for with

explanation.surface: A Milan football team battles with its crowd of spectators.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Audience' looks like the crowd at the match, but it means a formal meeting, as in an audience with the Pope.
explanation.definitionFit: An audience is a formal meeting granted by a dignitary, a kind of interview; the question mark flags the loose fit.

clue.text: Means to preserve obscure terms from the jazz age — oddly forget 'splitting'

indicators.note: terms are ends, so the last letter of each following word is taken
oddly keeps the letters in the odd positions only
splitting means forcing a way into the middle, so one piece sits inside the rest

blocks.note: deep can mean hard to understand, obscure
the last letters of the, jazz and age
the first, third and fifth letters of forget

explanation.surface: Someone wants to keep the obscure slang of the 1920s alive, while forgetting the old rule about split infinitives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Splitting' sounds like the grammar rule on split infinitives; it signals that the odd letters go between the other two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A deep-freeze is a freezer that keeps food for long periods, so it is a means of preserving.

clue.text: See 4
Things that burst out of star's trousers after length breaks fly

definitions.text: Things that burst out of star

indicators.note: breaks means breaking into, so one letter is inserted inside another word
after places the word before it second, behind the piece built from the rest

blocks.note: to soar is to fly high
L is the abbreviation for length
flares are trousers that widen below the knee

explanation.surface: A celebrity's trousers burst open at the fly, with things popping out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fly' reads as the trouser opening but means to rise through the air; flares are trousers that widen from the knee.
explanation.definitionFit: Solar flares are sudden eruptions of energy from the sun's surface, and the sun is a star.
